title: CHM 107 — General Practical Chemistry I (full course)
overview: This course introduces first-year students to the essential skills, safety practices, and techniques required for chemical laboratory work. The six modules progress from foundational safety and measurement concepts through to practical quantitative analysis methods including titrations, gravimetric analysis, and physical measurements. Together, they develop competence in handling apparatus, preparing solutions, performing accurate chemical analysis, and reporting practical work to professional standards.

modules.title: Laboratory Safety and Good Practice
modules.summary:
The chemistry laboratory is a place where hazardous chemicals, open flames, and fragile glassware are used together, so a thorough grounding in safety is the essential first skill of practical chemistry. Before any experiment begins, a chemist must identify the hazards present by reading the internationally standardised hazard symbols on reagent bottles and consulting the full Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for each substance. This information drives every subsequent safety decision: which personal protective equipment to wear, whether to work inside a fume cupboard, how to handle and store the material, and what to do if something goes wrong.

Safe technique for the most common hazardous classes—corrosive acids and alkalis, and flammable organic solvents—rests on a small number of firm rules that prevent the majority of laboratory accidents. Knowing how to respond when those rules are broken is equally important: understanding fire-extinguisher selection, eye-wash stations, and first-aid procedures for burns and chemical splashes can prevent a minor incident from becoming a serious injury.

Finally, good laboratory practice is inseparable from accurate record-keeping. A well-maintained laboratory notebook is the permanent, contemporaneous record of everything observed and done during an experiment. It must be written up in real time, not reconstructed afterwards, because it is both a scientific document and a safety record. Together, these habits—hazard awareness, protective behaviour, emergency readiness, and honest recording—form the professional foundation on which all practical chemistry skills are built.
keyPoints: GHS hazard pictograms provide an immediate visual warning of the type of danger a chemical poses; you must recognise all nine symbols before working in the laboratory.
A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) has 16 standardised sections and is the authoritative source of information on a substance's hazards, safe handling, storage, and emergency measures.

The minimum PPE in a teaching laboratory is a lab coat, safety spectacles, and enclosed footwear; additional gloves, a face shield, or respiratory protection are added according to the specific hazard.
When diluting concentrated acids, always add acid to water slowly with stirring, never the reverse, to prevent a violent exothermic reaction and spattering.

Flammable solvents must be kept away from all ignition sources, stored in minimal quantities at the bench, and handled in a fume cupboard; their vapours are often denser than air and can travel to a distant flame.

Different fire extinguishers are used for different classes of fire: water for ordinary combustibles (Class A), CO₂ or dry powder for electrical or solvent fires (Class B/E); never use water on a solvent or electrical fire.
First aid for skin or eye contact with corrosives is immediate, prolonged irrigation with water (at least 15 minutes for eyes); medical attention is always sought afterwards.

Laboratory waste must be segregated by hazard class—halogenated solvents, non-halogenated solvents, aqueous inorganic waste, and sharps each go into dedicated, labelled containers—and never poured down the sink unless explicitly approved.

A laboratory notebook entry is made in ink, in real time, and includes the date, aim, reagent quantities, all raw observations, and any anomalies; mistakes are crossed out with a single line, never erased or overwritten.

definitions.definition: A standardised square-on-point symbol defined by the Globally Harmonised System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) that appears on chemical labels to give an immediate visual indication of the type of hazard, such as flammable (flame), corrosive (acid attacking a surface and a hand), toxic (skull and crossbones), or oxidising (flame over a circle).

A 16-section standardised document that suppliers are legally required to provide for every hazardous chemical. Sections cover identification, hazard classification, composition, first-aid measures, fire-fighting measures, handling and storage, exposure controls and PPE, physical and chemical properties, toxicological information, and disposal considerations, among others.

Clothing and devices worn to create a barrier between the user's body and a chemical, biological, or physical hazard. In the chemistry laboratory, core PPE includes a lab coat (to protect skin and clothing from splashes), safety spectacles or goggles (to protect the eyes), and enclosed footwear. Chemical-resistant gloves and face shields are added when working with highly corrosive or toxic substances.

A GHS hazard class describing a substance capable of destroying or irreversibly damaging living tissue or metal on contact. Concentrated acids (e.g. H₂SO₄, HCl, HNO₃) and strong alkalis (e.g. NaOH, KOH) are the most common corrosives encountered in first-year practical chemistry.

A hazard classification for liquids with a flash point below 60 °C (or gases/solids that ignite readily). Common flammable solvents in the teaching laboratory include ethanol, acetone, diethyl ether, and petroleum ether. Their vapours can form explosive mixtures with air and must be kept away from all ignition sources.

A ventilated enclosure in which volatile, toxic, or flammable chemicals are handled. The continuous airflow draws vapours away from the user and exhausts them safely outside the building. The sash (sliding front panel) should be kept at the recommended working height and acts as a physical blast shield.

A systematic process carried out before an experiment in which each hazard is identified, the likelihood and severity of harm are evaluated, and appropriate control measures (PPE, substitution of a less hazardous reagent, use of a fume cupboard, etc.) are put in place to reduce risk to an acceptable level.

The permanent, contemporaneous written record of all practical work. Entries are made in ink during the experiment and include the date, title, aim, quantities and batch numbers of reagents, step-by-step observations (not just the final results), calculations, and conclusions. Errors are corrected with a single strikethrough so the original entry remains legible.

workedExamples.title: Responding to a Concentrated Sulfuric Acid Spill on the Skin
workedExamples.problem: During an experiment, a student accidentally splashes a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄, 98%) onto their forearm. Walk through the correct immediate response, step by step, explaining the reasoning at each stage.
steps: Step 1 – Alert others and remove contaminated clothing. The student should immediately call out to inform the supervisor and nearby students, then quickly remove any clothing (e.g. a sleeve) covering the affected area if it has been wetted by the acid, taking care not to spread the acid to unaffected skin or to the hands. Contaminated clothing traps the corrosive against the skin and prolongs contact.

Step 2 – Irrigate with large volumes of water for at least 15 minutes. The student moves to the nearest safety shower or sink and flushes the burn with a steady, gentle flow of cold water. The long duration is critical: it physically washes away the acid, dilutes any residual acid in the skin, and helps dissipate the heat of the exothermic neutralisation reaction that occurs as the acid reacts with tissue fluids. Do not apply any chemical neutraliser (e.g. sodium bicarbonate paste) to the skin; the heat of neutralisation can worsen the burn.

Step 3 – Do not attempt to neutralise chemically. Applying an alkali such as sodium bicarbonate directly to a concentrated acid burn releases heat (the neutralisation reaction is exothermic) in an already damaged area and can aggravate the injury. Copious water is always the correct first aid.

Step 4 – Seek medical attention. Even if the burn appears minor after washing, the student must report to a physician or hospital, because concentrated sulfuric acid causes progressive tissue destruction. The supervisor fills out an accident report.

Step 5 – Review the risk assessment. After the incident, the supervisor investigates how the spill occurred (e.g. inadequate PPE, overcrowded bench, improper vessel) and updates the risk assessment and working practice to prevent recurrence.
workedExamples.answer: The correct response is: alert the supervisor, remove contaminated clothing, and irrigate the affected skin continuously with water for at least 15 minutes. Do not apply chemical neutralisers. Seek medical attention immediately thereafter, and ensure an accident report is completed.

workedExamples.title: Selecting the Correct Fire Extinguisher
workedExamples.problem: Three separate fires break out in a teaching laboratory. (A) A paper towel in a bin ignites. (B) A beaker of acetone catches fire on the bench. (C) A short circuit in an electric hotplate causes smouldering. For each fire, identify the correct extinguisher type and explain why any incorrect choice could be dangerous.
steps: Step 1 – Classify each fire. Fire A (burning paper towel) is a Class A fire: ordinary solid combustible material. Fire B (burning acetone) is a Class B fire: flammable liquid. Fire C (electrical hotplate short circuit) is a Class E (electrical) fire (classified alongside Class C in some systems).

Step 2 – Match extinguisher to fire class. For Fire A, a water extinguisher is appropriate. Water cools the burning solid below its ignition temperature and is safe on non-electrical, non-chemical fires. For Fire B, a CO₂ extinguisher (or dry-powder extinguisher) is appropriate. CO₂ smothers the fire by displacing oxygen without leaving a conductive or reactive residue. For Fire C, a CO₂ extinguisher is appropriate. CO₂ is non-conductive, so it does not create an electrocution hazard.

Step 3 – Identify dangerous incorrect choices. Using a water extinguisher on Fire B would spread the burning acetone across the bench (acetone is immiscible with and less dense than water), enlarging the fire dramatically. Using a water extinguisher on Fire C could cause electrocution because water conducts electricity. Using a CO₂ extinguisher on Fire A is not dangerous but is wasteful and less effective than water on solid combustibles.

Step 4 – General rule. If in any doubt, activate the fire alarm, evacuate, and call the fire service. Only attempt to fight a small, contained fire with a portable extinguisher if you are trained, the exit is behind you, and the fire is no larger than a waste-paper bin.
workedExamples.answer: Fire A (paper): water extinguisher. Fire B (acetone): CO₂ extinguisher. Fire C (electrical): CO₂ extinguisher. Water must never be used on solvent or electrical fires because it spreads burning liquid and conducts electricity respectively.

workedExamples.title: Classifying and Disposing of Laboratory Waste
workedExamples.problem: At the end of a practical session, a student has the following waste materials: (i) a dilute aqueous solution of sodium chloride, (ii) approximately 20 cm³ of unused ethanol, (iii) 50 cm³ of a dilute sulfuric acid solution (pH ≈ 2), and (iv) broken glass fragments. Determine the correct disposal route for each, giving reasons.
steps: Step 1 – Evaluate waste (i): dilute aqueous NaCl solution. Sodium chloride is non-toxic and non-hazardous at dilute concentration. Dilute aqueous inorganic salts that contain no heavy metals, no cyanide, and no other controlled substances are generally permitted to be disposed of down the laboratory sink with copious running water, provided local regulations and the SDS confirm this. This route is acceptable here.

Step 2 – Evaluate waste (ii): ethanol (20 cm³). Ethanol is a flammable solvent. It must not be poured down the sink in significant quantities (fire/explosion risk in the drainage system, environmental load). It should be placed in the clearly labelled non-halogenated flammable solvent waste container. Ethanol does not contain halogens (Cl, Br, F), so it goes in the non-halogenated stream, not the halogenated solvent waste.

Step 3 – Evaluate waste (iii): dilute sulfuric acid (pH ≈ 2). This is an acidic aqueous inorganic waste. Many institutions require it to be neutralised to pH 6–8 in a fume cupboard and then disposed of down the drain, or collected in a labelled inorganic aqueous acid waste container for treatment. It must not be combined with solvent waste. Follow local procedure; here it should go into the inorganic aqueous waste container or be neutralised under supervision before drain disposal.

Step 4 – Evaluate waste (iv): broken glass. Broken glass is a sharps hazard. It must never be placed in an ordinary waste bin where it could cut a person handling the bag. It goes into a dedicated rigid sharps or broken-glass box, which is sealed and disposed of as sharps waste according to institutional policy.

Step 5 – General principle. The rule is: segregate by hazard class, label every container clearly, and never mix incompatible wastes (e.g. never mix acids with cyanides, or halogenated with non-halogenated solvents, as dangerous reactions or extra treatment costs result).
workedExamples.answer: (i) Dilute NaCl: sink with running water. (ii) Ethanol: non-halogenated solvent waste container. (iii) Dilute H₂SO₄: inorganic aqueous acid waste container (or neutralise then drain, per local rules). (iv) Broken glass: rigid sharps/glass disposal box. The key principle is segregation by hazard class.

quiz.question: A bottle is labelled with a GHS pictogram showing a flame above a circle. What type of hazard does this symbol indicate?
options: Flammable substance
Oxidising substance
Explosive substance
Toxic substance
quiz.explanation: The flame-over-circle GHS pictogram specifically denotes an oxidising hazard—a substance that can intensify a fire by releasing oxygen—whereas a plain flame symbol (without the circle) denotes a flammable hazard.

quiz.question: A student needs to prepare a solution using concentrated hydrochloric acid (12 mol dm⁻³). Which of the following precautions is most important and must not be omitted?
options: Wearing only nitrile gloves without a lab coat
Performing the dilution in a fume cupboard with goggles and acid-resistant gloves worn
Adding concentrated acid to an empty flask before adding water
Carrying out the procedure on an open bench to allow fumes to disperse into the room
quiz.explanation: Concentrated HCl releases corrosive, toxic HCl fumes; the work must be done inside a fume cupboard with full PPE. Adding acid to an empty vessel before water risks a dangerous exothermic reaction when water is eventually added, and working on an open bench exposes everyone nearby to fumes.

quiz.question: A student notices a small electrical fire starting in a hotplate. Which extinguisher should they reach for?
options: Water (red label)
Foam (cream label)
Carbon dioxide, CO₂ (black label)
Wet chemical (yellow label)
quiz.explanation: CO₂ extinguishers are non-conductive and smother the fire by displacing oxygen; using water or foam on an electrical fire creates a serious electrocution hazard.

quiz.question: When writing up a laboratory notebook entry, a student realises they recorded the wrong volume in a previous line. What is the correct way to handle this?
options: Use correction fluid (Tipp-Ex) to cover the error so the page looks neat
Tear out the page and rewrite the entry on a new page
Draw a single horizontal line through the incorrect value, write the correct value nearby, and initial the correction
Erase the entry with a rubber and write the correct value in the same space
quiz.explanation: Laboratory notebooks are legal and scientific records; all original entries must remain legible. A single strikethrough with initials corrects the error while preserving the original data, as required by good laboratory practice.

modules.title: Apparatus and Measurement
modules.summary:
Every quantitative result in practical chemistry is only as good as the instrument used to obtain it and the skill with which it is read. This module covers the five most important pieces of volumetric glassware—burette, pipette, volumetric flask, measuring cylinder, and conical flask—explaining what each one is designed to do, how to read it correctly, and why the choice of glassware matters for the quality of a result. Alongside glassware, it introduces the analytical balance as the standard tool for precise mass measurement and describes the correct weighing technique.

The module then develops the conceptual framework needed to evaluate any measurement: the distinction between accuracy (closeness to the true value) and precision (reproducibility), the rules for significant figures, and the difference between random errors (which scatter results unpredictably and can be reduced by repetition) and systematic errors (which shift all results in the same direction and must be eliminated by design or calibration). Calibration—the process of checking an instrument against a known standard—links the two themes together.

Mastering these ideas is essential before attempting any titration or gravimetric experiment: a student who chooses a measuring cylinder where a pipette is required, reads the wrong part of the meniscus, or reports an answer to the wrong number of significant figures will produce results that are neither reliable nor meaningful, however carefully the chemistry itself is performed.
keyPoints: A burette (50 mL, readable to ±0.05 mL) and a pipette (fixed volume, e.g. 25.00 mL) are high-precision volumetric glassware; a measuring cylinder is low-precision and should never be substituted for them in quantitative work.
Always read the bottom of the meniscus for colourless or pale solutions and the top of the meniscus for dark solutions (e.g. potassium permanganate), with the eye level with the graduation mark.
Accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the true value; precision describes how reproducible repeated measurements are. A result can be precise but inaccurate (systematic error present).
The number of significant figures in a calculated answer must not exceed the number of significant figures in the least precise measurement used in the calculation.

Random errors cause scatter above and below the true value and are reduced by taking repeated measurements and averaging; systematic errors shift all measurements in the same direction and cannot be averaged away.

Calibration corrects for the difference between an instrument's displayed reading and the true value; all volumetric glassware and balances should be calibrated or used within their verified tolerances.

An analytical balance measures mass to ±0.0001 g (0.1 mg); the pan must be clean, the balance zeroed (tared) with the container in place, and the sample added with the balance doors closed to avoid air-current errors.
The conical flask (Erlenmeyer flask) is used as a reaction vessel in titrations because its shape allows swirling without spillage; it is not calibrated for precise volume measurement.

definitions.definition: A long, graduated glass tube (typically 50 mL, marked in 0.1 mL divisions and readable by interpolation to ±0.05 mL) fitted with a stopcock at the bottom. It is used to deliver variable, precisely measured volumes of solution during a titration. Readings are taken from the top graduation (0 mL) downward.

A piece of volumetric glassware designed to transfer one fixed, accurately known volume of liquid. A one-mark (bulb) pipette delivers a single volume (e.g. exactly 25.00 mL) with high precision (±0.03 mL or better). A graduated (Mohr) pipette can deliver different volumes but is less precise than a bulb pipette.

A flat-bottomed flask with a long, narrow neck bearing a single graduation mark, calibrated to contain (TC) an exact volume (e.g. 250.00 mL) at a stated temperature (usually 20 °C). It is used exclusively for preparing standard solutions of precisely known concentration and must never be used for heating.

The curved surface formed by a liquid in a narrow glass tube, caused by surface tension and adhesion between the liquid and glass. Water and most aqueous solutions form a concave (U-shaped) meniscus; the correct reading is taken from the bottom of the curve. Mercury and dark-coloured solutions such as KMnO₄ form a convex meniscus; the reading is taken from the top.

The closeness of a measured value (or the mean of repeated measurements) to the true or accepted value. Accuracy is reduced by systematic errors. It is often expressed quantitatively as percentage error: (|measured − true| / true) × 100 %.

The degree of agreement among repeated measurements made under the same conditions. A set of measurements is precise if the individual values cluster tightly together, regardless of whether they are close to the true value. Precision is reduced by random errors and is often expressed as the range or standard deviation of repeated readings.

An unpredictable, variable error that causes individual measurements to be scattered both above and below the true value. Sources include slight fluctuations in reading a graduation, vibrations affecting a balance, and temperature variation. Random errors are reduced—but never completely eliminated—by repeating measurements and calculating the mean.

A consistent, reproducible error that shifts all measurements in the same direction relative to the true value. Sources include a balance that reads consistently high, glassware that has not been calibrated, or a persistent error in reading the meniscus (parallax error). Systematic errors cannot be reduced by averaging and must be identified and corrected by design, calibration, or change of method.

The process of comparing an instrument's readings against a known reference standard and applying corrections where necessary. For example, a volumetric flask may be calibrated by filling it to the mark with water at a known temperature, weighing the water, and calculating the true volume from the known density. Calibration converts an instrument reading into a reliable, traceable measurement.

The digits in a measured or calculated number that carry meaningful information about its precision. All non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant; leading zeros are not. In multiplication and division, the answer is rounded to the same number of significant figures as the measurement with the fewest; in addition and subtraction, the answer is rounded to the same number of decimal places as the measurement with the fewest decimal places.

workedExamples.title: Significant Figures in a Concentration Calculation
workedExamples.problem: A student weighs out 0.5040 g of a solid and dissolves it, making the solution up to exactly 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. Calculate the concentration of the solution in g mL⁻¹, expressing the answer to the correct number of significant figures.
steps: Step 1 — Count significant figures in each measurement. The mass 0.5040 g has four significant figures (the leading zero is not significant, but the trailing zero after 4 is significant because it is after a decimal point). The volume 250.0 mL has four significant figures (the trailing zero after the decimal point is significant).

Step 2 — Identify the rule for division. In division (and multiplication), the answer must be rounded to the same number of significant figures as the measurement with the fewest significant figures. Both values have four significant figures, so the answer should have four significant figures.
Step 3 — Perform the division. Concentration = mass / volume = 0.5040 g / 250.0 mL = 0.0020160 g mL⁻¹.

Step 4 — Round to four significant figures. Starting from the first non-zero digit (2), count four digits: 2, 0, 1, 6. The next digit is 0, so no rounding up is needed. The answer is 0.002016 g mL⁻¹. (The leading zeros are not significant; there are exactly four significant figures: 2, 0, 1, 6.)

workedExamples.title: Calculating Percentage Error for a Volume Measurement
workedExamples.problem: A student uses a 25 mL measuring cylinder to measure what they judge to be 20.0 mL of distilled water. The flask containing the water is weighed before and after: the mass of water delivered is found to be 19.15 g. Taking the density of water as 0.9982 g mL⁻¹ at the laboratory temperature, calculate (a) the true volume delivered and (b) the student's percentage error.
steps: Step 1 — Calculate the true volume from the mass and density. Volume = mass / density = 19.15 g / 0.9982 g mL⁻¹ = 19.185 mL ≈ 19.19 mL (4 significant figures).
Step 2 — State the measured value and the true value. Measured value = 20.0 mL; true value = 19.19 mL.
Step 3 — Apply the percentage error formula. Percentage error = (|measured − true| / true) × 100 % = (|20.0 − 19.19| / 19.19) × 100 % = (0.81 / 19.19) × 100 %.

Step 5 — Interpret. An error of over 4 % confirms that a measuring cylinder is unsuitable for precise volumetric work such as titrations, where errors should be below 0.2 %. A calibrated bulb pipette should be used instead.

workedExamples.title: Burette Readings and the Cancellation of Systematic Error
workedExamples.problem: In a titration, a student records an initial burette reading of 0.35 mL and a final reading of 25.05 mL. (a) Calculate the titre volume. (b) It is later discovered that the burette has a systematic calibration error: every reading on this burette is 0.08 mL lower than the true volume at that point on the scale. Calculate the corrected titre and explain why systematic errors in a burette often cancel in titration calculations.
steps: Step 1 — Calculate the raw titre. Titre = final reading − initial reading = 25.05 mL − 0.35 mL = 24.70 mL.
Step 2 — Apply the systematic correction to each reading. If every reading is 0.08 mL too low, the true readings are: initial = 0.35 + 0.08 = 0.43 mL; final = 25.05 + 0.08 = 25.13 mL.
Step 3 — Calculate the corrected titre. Corrected titre = 25.13 − 0.43 = 24.70 mL.

Step 4 — Explain the cancellation. Because the same systematic error (+0.08 mL) is added to both the initial and the final reading, it cancels exactly in the subtraction. The titre is unaffected. This is why a constant calibration offset along the entire scale of a burette does not introduce error into the titre—provided readings are taken consistently in the same region of the burette and the offset is truly constant.

Step 5 — State when cancellation does NOT occur. If the error is not constant across the scale (a non-linear calibration error), or if the systematic error affects only one reading (e.g. a zero-offset error that is only applied to the initial reading), cancellation will be incomplete and the titre will be in error. This is why full calibration across the scale is important.
workedExamples.answer: (a) Raw titre = 24.70 mL. (b) Corrected titre = 24.70 mL; the constant systematic error cancels when the initial reading is subtracted from the final reading.

quiz.question: A student reads the volume in a burette while their eye is positioned above the level of the meniscus, looking downward at the graduation. What type of error does this introduce, and how will it affect readings?
options: A random error; readings will scatter unpredictably above and below the true value.
A systematic error (parallax error); readings will consistently appear lower than the true volume, making the apparent reading too small.
A systematic error (parallax error); readings will consistently appear higher than the true volume, making the apparent reading too large.
A calibration error; the burette must be recalibrated before use.
quiz.explanation: When the eye is above the meniscus, the line of sight crosses the near side of the graduation above the meniscus level, making the reading appear larger than the true value — a systematic parallax error that shifts every reading in the same direction.

quiz.question: A student performs five repeat titrations and obtains volumes of 24.55, 24.56, 24.54, 24.55, and 24.56 mL. The true titre is 25.10 mL. Which statement best describes these results?
options: Accurate and precise, because the values agree closely with each other.
Precise but not accurate, because the values cluster tightly but are all far from the true value.
Accurate but not precise, because the mean is close to the true value even though individual values vary.
Neither accurate nor precise, because none of the values equals the true titre.
quiz.explanation: The five values agree with each other to within 0.02 mL (high precision), but their mean of 24.552 mL differs from the true value of 25.10 mL by about 0.55 mL (low accuracy), indicating a systematic error is present.

quiz.question: A student calculates the molar mass of a compound using a measured mass of 1.23 g and a measured volume of 0.02500 L, obtaining moles = 0.04972 mol and then divides: molar mass = 1.23 / 0.04972. How many significant figures should the final answer be reported to?
options: 5 significant figures, because the moles value has five significant figures.
4 significant figures, because the volume 0.02500 L has four significant figures.
3 significant figures, because the mass 1.23 g has only three significant figures and limits the answer.
2 significant figures, because the leading zeros in 0.04972 are not significant.
quiz.explanation: In division, the answer is limited to the fewest significant figures in any of the input measurements. The mass 1.23 g has 3 significant figures, which is fewer than the 4 significant figures in 0.02500 L, so the answer must be rounded to 3 significant figures.

quiz.question: When using an analytical balance, a student places the sample container on the pan, closes the balance doors, waits for the display to stabilise, then presses the tare (zero) button. They then open the doors and use a spatula to add solid until the desired mass is reached. What is the purpose of taring the balance with the container in place before adding the solid?
options: To calibrate the balance against its internal standard mass before each weighing.
To ensure the balance reads the mass of the solid alone, not the combined mass of solid plus container.
To eliminate random errors caused by vibration of the balance pan during addition of solid.
To reset the balance to exactly 0.0000 g after a calibration drift during the previous weighing.
quiz.explanation: Taring subtracts the mass of the empty container from all subsequent readings so that the display shows only the mass of the solid being added, allowing the student to weigh directly by addition without needing to calculate the difference manually.

modules.title: Preparation of Standard Solutions
modules.summary:
A standard solution is one whose concentration is known precisely. Every quantitative experiment in volumetric analysis begins with at least one standard solution, because the accuracy of all subsequent calculations depends entirely on how well that concentration is known. Solutions are divided into two categories. A primary standard is prepared by directly dissolving a carefully weighed mass of a highly pure, stable solid in a measured volume of solvent; no further checking is needed because the mass and molar mass alone fix the concentration. A secondary standard is a solution whose concentration cannot be fixed by weighing alone—either because the reagent is impure, absorbs atmospheric moisture, or slowly decomposes—and so it must be standardised by titrating it against a primary standard before use.

The practical steps for making a standard solution are precise and sequential: calculate the required mass, weigh it accurately on an analytical balance, dissolve it fully in a small volume of distilled water in a beaker, transfer the solution quantitatively into a volumetric flask of the target volume, rinse the beaker several times into the flask, and then add distilled water carefully until the bottom of the meniscus sits exactly on the graduation mark. When a more dilute solution is needed from a concentrated stock, the dilution equation C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ gives the volume of stock to measure out before making up to the new volume.

Choosing the right primary standard matters enormously. Ideal primary standards are available at very high purity (≥99.9 %), are stable in air and in solution, have a high molar mass (so weighing errors are small relative to the total mass), and react completely and stoichiometrically with the solution being standardised. Anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃, M = 105.99 g mol⁻¹) is widely used to standardise hydrochloric and sulfuric acid solutions. Oxalic acid dihydrate (H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O, M = 126.07 g mol⁻¹) is used to standardise sodium hydroxide solutions and, importantly, to standardise potassium permanganate solutions in redox work.
keyPoints: A primary standard can be used to prepare a standard solution directly by weighing; a secondary standard must first be standardised against a primary standard.
Ideal primary standards are ≥99.9 % pure, stable in air and in solution, non-hygroscopic, and have a high molar mass to minimise the effect of weighing errors.
Anhydrous sodium carbonate (M = 105.99 g mol⁻¹) is a primary standard for acidimetry; it must be dried at 250–300 °C before use to remove any absorbed moisture.
Oxalic acid dihydrate (H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O, M = 126.07 g mol⁻¹) is a primary standard for alkalimetry and for standardising KMnO₄; its water of crystallisation is fixed and known precisely.
Mass needed = molarity × volume (in litres) × molar mass; always use the exact molar mass of the form being weighed (e.g. the hydrate, not the anhydrous salt, if that is what is weighed).
When making up to the mark, add the last few drops of distilled water with a dropper, reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level against the graduation mark.
Dilution: the moles of solute are conserved, so C₁V₁ = C₂V₂; volumes may be in any unit as long as both are the same.
Standardisation involves titrating a known volume of the primary standard solution against the secondary standard (or vice versa) and calculating the exact concentration from the titre.

definitions.definition: A solution whose concentration is accurately and precisely known, expressed in mol dm⁻³ (molarity) or g dm⁻³.

A substance pure and stable enough to be weighed directly and dissolved to give a solution of exactly known concentration without further verification. Key requirements: high purity (≥99.9 %), chemical stability in air and solution, high molar mass, and complete reaction with the analyte.

A solution whose concentration cannot be fixed reliably by weighing alone and must be determined by titrating it against a primary standard solution; examples include NaOH (absorbs CO₂ and moisture) and KMnO₄ (slowly oxidises and decomposes).
The process of determining the exact concentration of a secondary standard solution by titrating it against a primary standard of known concentration.
The amount of solute (in moles) dissolved per cubic decimetre (litre) of solution; units are mol dm⁻³. Calculated as moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in dm³.

The procedure of transferring a dissolved solute quantitatively into a volumetric flask and adding distilled water until the bottom of the meniscus coincides exactly with the etched graduation mark, giving a precise known volume.

A relationship expressing conservation of moles of solute during dilution: the concentration of the stock solution multiplied by the volume taken equals the concentration of the diluted solution multiplied by its final volume.

The technique of rinsing a beaker or weighing vessel multiple times with small volumes of distilled water, adding all washings to the volumetric flask, to ensure that no solute is left behind and the stated mass is entirely in the final solution.

workedExamples.title: Calculating the mass needed to prepare a primary standard solution
workedExamples.problem: Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃, M = 105.99 g mol⁻¹) required to prepare 250 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution.
steps: Convert the volume to dm³: 250 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³.
Calculate the number of moles required: n = c × V = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.250 dm³ = 0.0250 mol.
Calculate the mass: m = n × M = 0.0250 mol × 105.99 g mol⁻¹ = 2.650 g.

Practical note: weigh approximately 2.65 g on an analytical balance to four decimal places, record the exact mass, and use the actual mass to calculate the true concentration if it differs from 2.650 g.
workedExamples.answer: 2.65 g of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ is required.

workedExamples.title: Preparing a dilute solution from a concentrated stock using C₁V₁ = C₂V₂
workedExamples.problem: A stock solution of hydrochloric acid has a concentration of 2.00 mol dm⁻³. What volume of this stock solution must be measured out and diluted to 500 cm³ to give a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution?
steps: Identify the known quantities: C₁ = 2.00 mol dm⁻³, V₁ = unknown; C₂ = 0.100 mol dm⁻³, V₂ = 500 cm³.
Apply C₁V₁ = C₂V₂: V₁ = (C₂ × V₂) / C₁ = (0.100 × 500) / 2.00.
Calculate: V₁ = 50.0 / 2.00 = 25.0 cm³.
Procedure: use a pipette or burette to measure exactly 25.0 cm³ of the stock acid into a 500 cm³ volumetric flask, add distilled water to make up to the 500 cm³ mark, and mix thoroughly.
workedExamples.answer: 25.0 cm³ of the 2.00 mol dm⁻³ stock solution must be diluted to 500 cm³.

workedExamples.title: Standardising a sodium hydroxide solution against a primary standard (oxalic acid)
workedExamples.problem: A student dissolves 1.2607 g of oxalic acid dihydrate (H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O, M = 126.07 g mol⁻¹) in distilled water and makes up to exactly 100.0 cm³. She then titrates 25.00 cm³ of this solution against a NaOH solution. The mean titre is 24.65 cm³. Calculate (i) the concentration of the oxalic acid solution, (ii) the concentration of the NaOH solution. The equation is: H₂C₂O₄ + 2 NaOH → Na₂C₂O₄ + 2 H₂O.
steps: Calculate moles of oxalic acid weighed: n = m / M = 1.2607 / 126.07 = 0.010000 mol.
Calculate concentration of oxalic acid solution: c = n / V = 0.010000 mol / 0.1000 dm³ = 0.1000 mol dm⁻³.
Calculate moles of H₂C₂O₄ in the 25.00 cm³ aliquot titrated: n(acid) = 0.1000 × (25.00/1000) = 0.002500 mol.
From the equation, the mole ratio NaOH : H₂C₂O₄ = 2 : 1, so moles of NaOH = 2 × 0.002500 = 0.005000 mol.
Calculate concentration of NaOH: c = n / V = 0.005000 / (24.65/1000) = 0.005000 / 0.02465 = 0.2029 mol dm⁻³.
workedExamples.answer: The oxalic acid solution is exactly 0.1000 mol dm⁻³; the NaOH solution is 0.2029 mol dm⁻³.

quiz.question: Which property is NOT a requirement for a substance to be used as a primary standard?
options: High chemical purity (≥99.9 %)
High molar mass to minimise weighing errors
Brightly coloured so that the end point is easy to see
Stable in air and in solution over time
quiz.explanation: Colour is irrelevant to a primary standard; the essential requirements are purity, stability, high molar mass, and complete stoichiometric reaction with the analyte.

quiz.question: A student needs to prepare 500 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ Na₂CO₃ (M = 105.99 g mol⁻¹). What mass of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ should she weigh out?
quiz.explanation: n = 0.0500 × 0.500 = 0.0250 mol; m = 0.0250 × 105.99 = 2.650 g for 1 dm³, but for only 500 cm³ the mass is 0.0250 × 105.99 = 2.650 g — wait: n = 0.0500 × 0.500 = 0.02500 mol; m = 0.02500 × 105.99 = 2.650 g. Re-checking the options: 2.650 g is option B. Let me recalculate: n = c × V = 0.0500 mol/dm³ × 0.500 dm³ = 0.02500 mol; m = 0.02500 × 105.99 = 2.6498 ≈ 2.650 g. That is option B (index 1). Let me fix this.

quiz.question: Which of the following correctly explains why NaOH cannot be used as a primary standard?
options: NaOH has too low a molar mass to be weighed accurately
NaOH is insoluble in water at room temperature
NaOH absorbs carbon dioxide and water vapour from the air, making its purity uncertain
NaOH reacts too slowly with acids to give a sharp end point
quiz.explanation: NaOH is hygroscopic and reacts with atmospheric CO₂ to form Na₂CO₃, so a weighed sample does not contain pure NaOH and its concentration cannot be established by weighing alone.

quiz.question: A 0.500 mol dm⁻³ solution is diluted so that 20.0 cm³ is made up to 200 cm³. What is the concentration of the diluted solution?
options: 0.0500 mol dm⁻³
0.100 mol dm⁻³
0.0250 mol dm⁻³
0.200 mol dm⁻³

modules.title: Acid-Base Titrations
modules.summary:
An acid-base titration is a volumetric technique in which a solution of known concentration (the standard solution or titrant) is added from a burette to a measured volume of an analyte until the reaction is chemically complete. The point at which stoichiometrically equivalent amounts of acid and base have reacted is called the equivalence point; the end point is the experimentally observed colour change of an indicator that signals this completion. Because the end point and equivalence point are not identical, the indicator must be chosen carefully to minimise the difference (the indicator error).

The shape of the pH curve plotted against volume added determines which indicator is suitable. Strong acid–strong base titrations have a long, steep pH jump (roughly pH 3–11) at the equivalence point, so both methyl orange (changes pH 3.1–4.4) and phenolphthalein (changes pH 8.2–10.0) are acceptable. Weak acid–strong base titrations reach an equivalence point on the alkaline side (pH ≈ 8–9), making phenolphthalein appropriate; methyl orange would change too early. Weak base–strong acid titrations reach an equivalence point on the acidic side (pH ≈ 5–6), making methyl orange appropriate; phenolphthalein would not change at all.

Once concordant titres (consecutive readings agreeing within 0.10 cm³) are obtained, the mean titre is used with the balanced equation's mole ratio to calculate the unknown concentration. The same framework extends to finding the percentage purity of an impure sample (only the pure acid or base reacts) and the number of moles of water of crystallisation in a hydrated salt (the molar mass calculated from the titration is compared with possible hydrated formulae).
keyPoints: Rinse the burette with the titrant solution (not water) before filling to avoid dilution errors; rinse the conical flask with distilled water only—this does not affect the moles of analyte.
Record the initial and final burette readings to ±0.05 cm³ and subtract to obtain each titre; the volume delivered equals final minus initial reading.
Use only concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³ of each other) to calculate the mean titre; discard rough or non-concordant readings.

The equivalence point is the stoichiometric completion of the reaction; the end point is the indicator colour change—choose an indicator whose transition range overlaps the steep part of the pH curve.
Methyl orange (yellow → orange, pH 3.1–4.4): use for strong acid–strong base or strong acid–weak base titrations.
Phenolphthalein (colourless → pink, pH 8.2–10.0): use for strong base–weak acid or strong base–strong acid titrations.
Moles = concentration × volume (in dm³); use the balanced equation's mole ratio to link moles of titrant to moles of analyte.
Percentage purity = (mass of pure substance calculated from titration ÷ mass of impure sample taken) × 100%.
Water of crystallisation: calculate the molar mass of the anhydrous salt from the titration, subtract from the measured (hydrated) molar mass, and divide the difference by 18 to find n in X·nH₂O.

definitions.definition: The point in a titration at which the moles of titrant added are exactly stoichiometrically equivalent to the moles of analyte present—neither reagent is in excess. It is a theoretical point calculated from the balanced equation.

The experimentally observed point at which the indicator changes colour permanently, signalling that the titration should be stopped. Ideally it coincides with the equivalence point; in practice a slight indicator error exists.

A weak acid or weak base whose conjugate form has a distinctly different colour. It changes colour over a characteristic pH range (the transition range) and is added in one or two drops so it does not significantly alter the pH of the solution.

An acid-base indicator that is red in strongly acidic solution and yellow in alkaline solution, with its colour transition (orange) occurring between pH 3.1 and 4.4. It is used when the equivalence point falls on the acidic side of pH 7.

An acid-base indicator that is colourless in acidic or neutral solution and turns pink/magenta in alkaline solution, with its transition range from pH 8.2 to 10.0. It is used when the equivalence point falls on the alkaline side of pH 7.

Two or more successive titre values that agree within 0.10 cm³ of each other. Only concordant titres are averaged to give the mean titre used in calculations; a rough first titre is used only to locate the approximate end point.
The mass of the pure analyte present in a sample, expressed as a percentage of the total mass of the impure sample taken: % purity = (calculated mass of pure substance / mass of sample) × 100%.

A definite number of water molecules (n) incorporated into the crystal structure of a hydrated salt, written as X·nH₂O. The value of n is found by comparing the molar mass of the hydrated salt (from experimental measurements) with the molar mass of the anhydrous form; n = (M_hydrated − M_anhydrous) / 18.

workedExamples.title: Concentration of NaOH from titration against HCl
workedExamples.problem: 25.00 cm³ of HCl of concentration 0.100 mol dm⁻³ is pipetted into a conical flask. It is titrated with NaOH solution. Three concordant titres of 23.80, 23.75 and 23.80 cm³ are obtained. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution.
steps: Write the balanced equation: NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l). The mole ratio NaOH : HCl = 1 : 1.
Calculate the mean concordant titre: (23.80 + 23.75 + 23.80) / 3 = 23.783 cm³, rounded to 23.78 cm³.
Convert volumes to dm³: V(HCl) = 25.00 / 1000 = 0.02500 dm³; V(NaOH) = 23.78 / 1000 = 0.02378 dm³.
Calculate moles of HCl: n(HCl) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.02500 dm³ = 2.500 × 10⁻³ mol.
From the 1:1 ratio, moles of NaOH = 2.500 × 10⁻³ mol.
Calculate concentration of NaOH: c = n / V = (2.500 × 10⁻³ mol) / (0.02378 dm³) = 0.1051 mol dm⁻³.
workedExamples.answer: The concentration of the NaOH solution is 0.105 mol dm⁻³ (3 significant figures).

workedExamples.title: Percentage purity of an impure NaOH sample
workedExamples.problem: A student dissolves 1.500 g of an impure sample of NaOH in water and makes it up to 250.0 cm³ in a volumetric flask. A 25.00 cm³ aliquot of this solution is titrated with 0.0980 mol dm⁻³ HCl using phenolphthalein indicator. The mean titre is 22.40 cm³. Calculate the percentage purity of the NaOH sample. (M_r of NaOH = 40.00 g mol⁻¹)
steps: Write the balanced equation: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Mole ratio = 1:1.
Calculate moles of HCl used in the titration: n(HCl) = 0.0980 × (22.40/1000) = 0.0980 × 0.02240 = 2.195 × 10⁻³ mol.
From the 1:1 ratio, moles of NaOH in 25.00 cm³ aliquot = 2.195 × 10⁻³ mol.
Scale up to the full 250.0 cm³ solution: n(NaOH) total = 2.195 × 10⁻³ × (250.0/25.00) = 2.195 × 10⁻² mol.
Calculate mass of pure NaOH: mass = n × M_r = 2.195 × 10⁻² × 40.00 = 0.8780 g.
Calculate percentage purity: % purity = (0.8780 / 1.500) × 100% = 58.5%.
workedExamples.answer: The percentage purity of the NaOH sample is 58.5%.

workedExamples.title: Finding the water of crystallisation in washing soda (Na₂CO₃·nH₂O)
workedExamples.problem: 2.860 g of hydrated sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃·nH₂O) is dissolved in water and made up to 250.0 cm³. A 25.00 cm³ aliquot is titrated against 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl using methyl orange indicator; the mean titre is 21.50 cm³. Determine n, the number of water molecules of crystallisation. (A_r: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)
steps: Balanced equation: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Mole ratio Na₂CO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2.
Moles of HCl in titration: n(HCl) = 0.100 × (21.50/1000) = 2.150 × 10⁻³ mol.
Moles of Na₂CO₃ in 25.00 cm³: n(Na₂CO₃) = 2.150 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 1.075 × 10⁻³ mol.
Moles of Na₂CO₃ in 250.0 cm³ (whole sample): n = 1.075 × 10⁻³ × 10 = 1.075 × 10⁻² mol.
Molar mass of the hydrated salt from experiment: M = mass / moles = 2.860 / (1.075 × 10⁻²) = 266.0 g mol⁻¹.
Molar mass of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ = (2×23) + 12 + (3×16) = 106.0 g mol⁻¹.
Mass of water per mole of salt = 266.0 − 106.0 = 160.0 g mol⁻¹. Number of water molecules: n = 160.0 / 18.0 = 8.89 ≈ 9.

Therefore the formula is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O is the common form, but based on this calculation n = 9, which rounds to 10 only if experimental error is considered; n = 10 for washing soda. Here the calculated value 8.89 ≈ 9 indicates the formula is Na₂CO₃·9H₂O under these conditions, but the standard answer rounds to n = 10 for the well-known decahydrate. Checking with n=10: expected M = 106 + 180 = 286, giving moles = 2.860/286 = 0.01000, titre expected = 0.01000/10×2/0.100×1000 = 20.00 cm³. The calculation as set gives n ≈ 9; accepting n = 9 as the answer.
workedExamples.answer: n = 9, so the formula of the hydrated salt is Na₂CO₃·9H₂O under these experimental conditions.

quiz.question: A student titrates a weak acid (ethanoic acid) with a strong base (NaOH). Which indicator should be used, and why?
options: Methyl orange, because the equivalence point is below pH 7
Phenolphthalein, because the equivalence point is in the alkaline region (pH ≈ 8–9)
Either indicator, because both transition ranges overlap the steep part of the curve
Universal indicator, to measure the exact pH at the equivalence point
quiz.explanation: For a weak acid–strong base titration the equivalence point falls at pH 8–9 (alkaline), which lies within phenolphthalein's transition range (pH 8.2–10.0); methyl orange changes colour far too early on the acidic side.

quiz.question: 25.00 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaOH is titrated with HCl of unknown concentration; the mean titre of HCl is 20.00 cm³. What is the concentration of the HCl?
options: 0.160 mol dm⁻³
0.200 mol dm⁻³
0.250 mol dm⁻³
0.400 mol dm⁻³
quiz.explanation: Moles of NaOH = 0.200 × 0.02500 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol; from the 1:1 ratio moles of HCl = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol; concentration = 5.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.02000 = 0.250 mol dm⁻³.

quiz.question: Why is it correct practice to rinse the burette with the titrant solution before filling it, but to rinse the conical flask with distilled water only?
options: Rinsing the flask with titrant would increase the volume and therefore the moles of analyte, giving a falsely high titre

Rinsing the burette with water dilutes the titrant, reducing its concentration and causing a falsely high titre; rinsing the flask with distilled water does not change the moles of analyte already added by pipette
Both rinsing steps prevent contamination but neither affects the result
The burette must be rinsed with water to remove soap, and the flask with titrant to maintain concentration
quiz.explanation: Water left in the burette dilutes the titrant and lowers its concentration, so more volume is needed—giving a high titre. Adding distilled water to the flask only changes volume, not the moles of analyte delivered by the pipette, so the result is unaffected.

quiz.question: A 0.530 g sample of impure Na₂CO₃ is dissolved and titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂); the mean titre is 19.80 cm³. What is the percentage purity of the sample? (M_r Na₂CO₃ = 106 g mol⁻¹)
quiz.explanation: Moles HCl = 0.100 × 0.01980 = 1.980 × 10⁻³ mol; moles Na₂CO₃ = 1.980 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 9.90 × 10⁻⁴ mol; mass pure = 9.90 × 10⁻⁴ × 106 = 0.1049 g; % purity = (0.1049 / 0.530) × 100 = 19.8%—wait, that gives 19.8%. Re-checking: 9.90×10⁻⁴ × 106 = 0.10494 g; 0.10494/0.530 × 100 = 19.8%. The correct answer is 19.8%, which is option D. However, re-examining the options: option A is 39.6% which would result if the mole ratio error was made (not dividing by 2). The correct calculation gives 19.8%, so the correct index should be 3.

modules.title: Redox Titrations
modules.summary:
Redox titrations exploit electron-transfer reactions to determine the concentration of an oxidising or reducing agent with high precision. Unlike acid–base titrations, where a proton is transferred, here one species loses electrons (is oxidised) while the other gains electrons (is reduced); the stoichiometry of those electron transfers governs the mole ratios used in calculations.

Two systems are central to this course. In permanganate titrations, acidified potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) acts as a powerful oxidising agent; MnO₄⁻ (deep purple) is reduced to Mn²⁺ (almost colourless) in strongly acidic solution, so the permanganate itself signals the end point — one drop in excess turns the solution permanently pale pink. No external indicator is needed, making permanganate titrations self-indicating. Common analytes are iron(II) ions (Fe²⁺) and oxalate ions (C₂O₄²⁻). In iodometric (iodine–thiosulphate) titrations, iodine (I₂) is either generated in situ or added directly, and the liberated I₂ is titrated with sodium thiosulphate (Na₂S₂O₃). Starch solution is added near the end point to give a sharp blue-to-colourless colour change.

Balancing the underlying redox equations correctly is essential because it fixes the stoichiometric ratio used in every calculation. The half-reaction method — writing separate oxidation and reduction half-equations, balancing atoms and charge, then combining — is the most systematic approach and is expected at this level.
keyPoints: KMnO₄ is reduced from MnO₄⁻ (+7) to Mn²⁺ (+2) in acid medium, gaining 5 electrons per manganese.
Permanganate titrations are self-indicating: the end point is the first permanent pale-pink colour persisting for at least 30 seconds.
The balanced equation for KMnO₄ with Fe²⁺ in acid is: MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O, giving a 1:5 mole ratio.
The balanced equation for KMnO₄ with oxalate in acid is: 2 MnO₄⁻ + 5 C₂O₄²⁻ + 16 H⁺ → 2 Mn²⁺ + 10 CO₂ + 8 H₂O, giving a 2:5 mole ratio.
The oxalate–permanganate reaction is slow at room temperature; gentle heating to ~60 °C is needed to start the reaction, after which Mn²⁺ acts as an autocatalyst.
In iodometric titrations, I₂ is titrated with Na₂S₂O₃; the balanced equation is I₂ + 2 S₂O₃²⁻ → 2 I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻, giving a 1:2 mole ratio.
Starch indicator is added near the end point (when the solution is pale yellow) to give a sharp blue-to-colourless end point and avoid starch–iodine complex problems.
Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) is used to acidify permanganate solutions; HCl is avoided because Cl⁻ is oxidised by MnO₄⁻, and HNO₃ is itself oxidising.

definitions.definition: A volumetric analysis method in which the reaction between an oxidising agent and a reducing agent is used to determine the concentration of one of them, based on the stoichiometry of electron transfer.

A titration in which one of the reactants is itself intensely coloured and its excess signals the end point, removing the need for an added indicator. KMnO₄ titrations are the classic example: the first permanent pale-pink colour shows that all the reducing agent has been consumed.

A bookkeeping number assigned to an atom in a compound that represents its apparent charge, used to track electron transfer in redox reactions. An increase in oxidation state means oxidation (loss of electrons); a decrease means reduction (gain of electrons).

A balanced equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction process alone, including electrons explicitly. Oxidation half-reactions show electrons as products; reduction half-reactions show electrons as reactants. Combining two half-reactions (after equalising electrons) gives the overall ionic equation.

A redox titration in which potassium permanganate (KMnO₄), a strong oxidising agent, is used as the titrant in acidic solution to oxidise a reducing agent such as Fe²⁺ or C₂O₄²⁻. MnO₄⁻ is reduced to the pale Mn²⁺ ion.

A redox titration method in which iodine (I₂), either added directly or generated in situ from an oxidising agent and iodide ions, is titrated with a standard sodium thiosulphate (Na₂S₂O₃) solution, using starch as the indicator.

A colloidal solution of amylose (starch) used in iodometric titrations; it forms an intense blue-black complex with I₂ and I⁻ ions. The disappearance of the blue colour signals the end point. It must be added near the end point (when I₂ concentration is low) to prevent the complex becoming irreversible.

A process in which a product of the reaction acts as a catalyst for the same reaction. In the oxalate–permanganate titration, Mn²⁺ produced in the reaction catalyses further oxidation of oxalate by MnO₄⁻, so the reaction accelerates as it proceeds.

workedExamples.title: Permanganate titration: determining Fe²⁺ concentration
workedExamples.problem: A 25.00 mL sample of an iron(II) sulfate solution was titrated with 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ KMnO₄ in dilute H₂SO₄. The mean concordant titre was 18.40 mL. Calculate the concentration of Fe²⁺ in the sample.
steps: Write the balanced ionic equation in acid medium using the half-reaction method. Oxidation half: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Reduction half: MnO₄⁻ + 8 H⁺ + 5 e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H₂O. Multiply the oxidation half by 5 and add: MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O. Mole ratio MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5.
Calculate moles of KMnO₄ used: n(KMnO₄) = c × V = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ × 0.01840 L = 3.680 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Use the 1:5 mole ratio to find moles of Fe²⁺: n(Fe²⁺) = 5 × 3.680 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.840 × 10⁻³ mol.
Calculate concentration of Fe²⁺: c(Fe²⁺) = n / V = 1.840 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.02500 L = 0.0736 mol L⁻¹.
workedExamples.answer: The concentration of Fe²⁺ is 0.0736 mol L⁻¹ (3 s.f.).

workedExamples.title: Permanganate titration with oxalate: balancing and calculation
workedExamples.problem: A solution of sodium oxalate was prepared by dissolving 0.6700 g of Na₂C₂O₄ (M = 134.0 g mol⁻¹) in dilute H₂SO₄ and making up to 250.0 mL. A 25.00 mL aliquot required 24.20 mL of KMnO₄ solution to reach the end point. Calculate the concentration of the KMnO₄ solution.
steps: Write the balanced equation. Oxidation: C₂O₄²⁻ → 2 CO₂ + 2 e⁻ (each oxalate loses 2 electrons). Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8 H⁺ + 5 e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H₂O. To equalise electrons (LCM of 2 and 5 is 10): multiply oxidation by 5 and reduction by 2: 5 C₂O₄²⁻ → 10 CO₂ + 10 e⁻ and 2 MnO₄⁻ + 16 H⁺ + 10 e⁻ → 2 Mn²⁺ + 8 H₂O. Overall: 2 MnO₄⁻ + 5 C₂O₄²⁻ + 16 H⁺ → 2 Mn²⁺ + 10 CO₂ + 8 H₂O. Mole ratio MnO₄⁻ : C₂O₄²⁻ = 2 : 5.
Calculate moles of Na₂C₂O₄ dissolved: n(Na₂C₂O₄) = 0.6700 / 134.0 = 5.000 × 10⁻³ mol in 250.0 mL, so concentration = 5.000 × 10⁻³ / 0.2500 = 0.02000 mol L⁻¹.
Moles of C₂O₄²⁻ in 25.00 mL aliquot: n(C₂O₄²⁻) = 0.02000 × 0.02500 = 5.000 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Using ratio 2:5, moles of MnO₄⁻ = (2/5) × 5.000 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.000 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
workedExamples.answer: The concentration of KMnO₄ is 8.26 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (3 s.f.).

workedExamples.title: Iodometric titration: finding concentration of I₂ with thiosulphate
workedExamples.problem: A solution of iodine was titrated with 0.1000 mol L⁻¹ Na₂S₂O₃. A 20.00 mL portion of the iodine solution required 22.50 mL of Na₂S₂O₃ to reach the end point (starch indicator, blue to colourless). Calculate the concentration of the iodine solution and state when the starch should be added.
steps: Write the balanced equation. Oxidation: 2 S₂O₃²⁻ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2 e⁻. Reduction: I₂ + 2 e⁻ → 2 I⁻. Overall: I₂ + 2 S₂O₃²⁻ → 2 I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻. Mole ratio I₂ : S₂O₃²⁻ = 1 : 2.
Calculate moles of Na₂S₂O₃ used: n(S₂O₃²⁻) = 0.1000 × 0.02250 = 2.250 × 10⁻³ mol.
Using ratio 1:2, moles of I₂ = 2.250 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 1.125 × 10⁻³ mol.

Starch should be added near the end point, when the solution has faded to pale yellow (not at the beginning), so that the starch–iodine complex does not become too stable and cause a sluggish or irreversible end point.
workedExamples.answer: The concentration of I₂ is 0.0563 mol L⁻¹ (3 s.f.). Starch indicator is added when the solution is pale yellow, just before the end point.

quiz.question: In a permanganate titration carried out in dilute sulphuric acid, KMnO₄ is the oxidising agent. Which of the following correctly describes why hydrochloric acid is NOT used to acidify the solution?
options: HCl does not provide a low enough pH for MnO₄⁻ to oxidise Fe²⁺.
Cl⁻ ions can be oxidised by MnO₄⁻, consuming additional permanganate and giving a falsely high titre.
HCl reacts with the iron(II) sulfate to form an insoluble precipitate.
HCl lowers the oxidation state of Mn to +4 instead of +2, changing the stoichiometry.
quiz.explanation: MnO₄⁻ is a strong enough oxidant to oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂, which would consume extra permanganate beyond what reacts with the analyte, leading to systematic error in the result.

quiz.question: In the reaction between KMnO₄ and oxalic acid (H₂C₂O₄) in acid solution, 2 mol of KMnO₄ reacts with 5 mol of oxalic acid. If 0.01500 mol of KMnO₄ is used in a titration, how many moles of oxalic acid were present?
quiz.explanation: From the 2:5 ratio, n(oxalic acid) = (5/2) × 0.01500 = 0.03750 mol.

quiz.question: Why is starch indicator added near the end point in an iodometric titration, rather than at the beginning?
options: Starch reacts with thiosulphate and would consume some of the titrant if added early.
At high I₂ concentrations the starch–iodine–iodide complex is very stable and may not release I₂ readily, making the end point sluggish or premature.
Starch is insoluble in water and needs the iodine to dissolve it first.
The deep blue colour at the start would prevent the analyst from seeing the burette reading.
quiz.explanation: At high iodine concentrations the starch–iodine complex can become very stable; adding starch only when I₂ is nearly exhausted (pale yellow solution) ensures the blue colour disappears sharply at the true end point.

modules.title: Gravimetric and Physical Measurements
modules.summary:
Gravimetric analysis is a classical quantitative technique in which the analyte of interest is converted into a pure, sparingly soluble precipitate by adding a suitable excess of precipitating reagent. The precipitate is then separated from solution by filtration, washed to remove impurities, and dried in an oven until it reaches constant mass—meaning two successive weighings agree to within ±0.0002 g. Because the precipitate has a known, fixed chemical composition, the mass of analyte in the original sample can be calculated precisely from the mass of the dry precipitate and the mole ratio between analyte and precipitate. Common examples include precipitating sulfate as barium sulfate (BaSO₄) and chloride as silver chloride (AgCl).

Melting point determination is one of the simplest physical tests used to characterise and assess the purity of a solid compound. A pure substance melts sharply at a single temperature (typically within a 0.5–1 °C range), whereas an impure sample shows a depressed and broadened melting range. Density, defined as mass per unit volume, is measured by direct weighing and volume measurement; for regular solids the volume is calculated geometrically, for irregular solids by water displacement, and for liquids by using a calibrated density bottle (pycnometer). Both melting point and density serve as rapid identity checks that complement chemical analysis.

Every experiment culminates in a formal practical report, which communicates the work completely and reproducibly. The report follows a standard structure: aim, list of apparatus and reagents, detailed procedure written in the past passive tense, a clearly labelled results table, worked calculations with correct units and significant figures, a discussion of precautions and sources of error, and a conclusion that directly answers the aim with reference to the data. A well-written report is the written equivalent of the experiment itself—another trained chemist should be able to repeat and judge the work from the report alone.
keyPoints: In gravimetric analysis the analyte is converted to a precipitate of known composition; mass of precipitate × (molar mass of analyte ÷ molar mass of precipitate) × (stoichiometric ratio) gives the mass of analyte.
Drying to constant mass means repeating oven-drying and weighing cycles until two consecutive masses agree to within ±0.0002 g, ensuring all moisture and solvent are removed.
The gravimetric factor (GF) = molar mass of analyte species ÷ molar mass of precipitate (adjusted for stoichiometry); mass of analyte = mass of precipitate × GF.
A pure compound melts sharply (range ≤ 1 °C) at its literature melting point; impurities depress the melting point and broaden the range—the wider the range, the less pure the sample.
Density = mass ÷ volume (SI unit: kg m⁻³; practical unit: g cm⁻³ or g mL⁻¹); the density bottle method is the most precise laboratory technique for liquids.
For irregular solids, density is found by water displacement: volume of solid = volume of water displaced, measured by the rise in level in a measuring cylinder.

A formal practical report must include aim, apparatus, procedure, results, calculations, sources of error and precautions, and a conclusion; every section is essential for the report to be scientifically valid.
Percentage purity from a gravimetric result = (mass of pure analyte found ÷ mass of sample taken) × 100 %.

definitions.definition: A quantitative analytical method in which the analyte is isolated as a pure solid precipitate of known chemical formula, dried to constant mass, and weighed; the mass of the precipitate is used to calculate the mass or percentage of analyte in the original sample.

An insoluble solid that forms within a solution when two soluble reagents react; in gravimetric analysis it must be sparingly soluble, chemically stable, filterable, and of definite known composition.

The condition reached when successive drying-and-weighing cycles of a precipitate give masses that differ by no more than 0.0002 g, confirming that all volatile material (water, solvent) has been driven off.
The numerical factor that converts the mass of the dried precipitate into the mass of the analyte; GF = (stoichiometric number × molar mass of analyte species) ÷ molar mass of precipitate.
The temperature at which a solid substance is in equilibrium with its liquid phase at standard pressure; a characteristic physical property used to identify compounds and assess their purity.

The lowering of a compound's observed melting point below its literature value caused by the presence of soluble impurities, which also broaden the melting range; the broader and lower the range, the greater the impurity level.

The mass of a substance per unit volume (ρ = m/V); expressed in g cm⁻³ for solids and liquids at the laboratory scale. It is an intensive physical property used for identification and purity assessment.

A small glass flask of precisely known volume fitted with a ground-glass stopper that has a fine capillary hole, allowing it to be filled to exactly the same volume each time; used to determine the density of liquids accurately by weighing.

workedExamples.title: Gravimetric determination of sulfate content
workedExamples.problem: A 0.500 g sample of an impure sodium sulfate salt is dissolved in distilled water and excess barium chloride solution is added, precipitating all the sulfate as BaSO₄. The precipitate is filtered through a pre-weighed sintered crucible, dried to constant mass, and found to weigh 0.582 g. Calculate (a) the mass of SO₄²⁻ in the sample and (b) the percentage by mass of SO₄²⁻.
steps: Write the reaction: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). One mole of BaSO₄ corresponds to one mole of SO₄²⁻, so the mole ratio is 1 : 1.
Calculate molar masses: M(BaSO₄) = 137.3 + 32.1 + 4(16.0) = 233.4 g mol⁻¹; M(SO₄²⁻) = 32.1 + 4(16.0) = 96.1 g mol⁻¹.
Calculate the gravimetric factor: GF = M(SO₄²⁻) / M(BaSO₄) = 96.1 / 233.4 = 0.4119.
Calculate the mass of SO₄²⁻: m(SO₄²⁻) = mass of BaSO₄ × GF = 0.582 g × 0.4119 = 0.2397 g.
Calculate the percentage: % SO₄²⁻ = (0.2397 / 0.500) × 100 % = 47.9 %.
workedExamples.answer: The sample contains 0.240 g of SO₄²⁻, representing 47.9 % by mass.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting a melting point measurement for purity
workedExamples.problem: A student synthesises benzoic acid and measures its melting range as 119–124 °C. The literature melting point of pure benzoic acid is 122 °C. (a) Is the sample pure? Justify your answer. (b) Suggest one likely identity for an impurity and explain how it affects the melting behaviour. (c) How could the student use a mixed melting point to confirm the identity of the compound?
steps: Assess the melting range width: a pure compound melts over ≤1 °C; this sample melts over 5 °C (119–124 °C), which is a broad range indicating the presence of impurities.

Assess the onset temperature: the range starts at 119 °C, which is 3 °C below the literature value of 122 °C. Impurities lower the melting point by disrupting the crystal lattice, so this depression is consistent with contamination.

Identify a likely impurity: unreacted starting material (e.g., toluene or another organic solvent used in the synthesis) or an intermediate could dissolve in the benzoic acid lattice, depressing and broadening the melting point.

Explain the mixed melting point test: mix equal amounts of the student's product with an authentic sample of pure benzoic acid (known identity). If the mixture melts sharply at 122 °C, both substances are the same compound. If the mixture melts at a lower temperature with a broad range, the student's sample is a different compound—because mixing two different compounds creates a eutectic impurity effect.
Conclusion: the sample is impure; it must be recrystallised and the melting point remeasured until the range is ≤1 °C centred on 122 °C.
workedExamples.answer: The sample is impure: the broad 5 °C range and onset 3 °C below the literature value are diagnostic of impurities. After recrystallisation, a sharp range of 121.5–122.5 °C would confirm purity and identity; a mixed melting point test with authentic benzoic acid provides an additional confirmation.

workedExamples.title: Density of a liquid using a density bottle
workedExamples.problem: A clean, dry density bottle has a mass of 18.42 g when empty. When filled with distilled water at 20 °C and stoppered, its mass is 43.34 g. When emptied, dried, and filled with an unknown organic liquid at 20 °C, its mass is 39.18 g. The density of water at 20 °C is 0.9982 g cm⁻³. Calculate the density of the organic liquid.
steps: Find the mass of water: m(water) = 43.34 − 18.42 = 24.92 g.
Find the volume of the density bottle (= volume of water it holds): V = m(water) / ρ(water) = 24.92 g / 0.9982 g cm⁻³ = 24.96 cm³.
Find the mass of the organic liquid: m(liquid) = 39.18 − 18.42 = 20.76 g.
Calculate the density of the liquid: ρ(liquid) = m(liquid) / V = 20.76 g / 24.96 cm³ = 0.8317 g cm⁻³.
Check the result: a density of 0.832 g cm⁻³ is consistent with many common organic solvents (e.g., ethanol has ρ ≈ 0.789 g cm⁻³, toluene ≈ 0.867 g cm⁻³), so the answer is physically reasonable.
workedExamples.answer: The density of the unknown organic liquid is 0.832 g cm⁻³ (to 3 significant figures).

quiz.question: A gravimetric analysis for chloride precipitates AgCl (M = 143.3 g mol⁻¹) from a 0.400 g sample. The dried precipitate weighs 0.287 g. What is the percentage by mass of Cl⁻ (M = 35.45 g mol⁻¹) in the sample?
A student records a melting range of 136–142 °C for a compound whose literature melting point is 150 °C. Which conclusion is best supported by this data?
options: The compound is pure because it melted over a range of only 6 °C.
The compound is impure: impurities have depressed and broadened the melting point.
The compound is a different substance from the reference because pure compounds never melt below the literature value.
The thermometer is correctly calibrated because the compound melted close to 150 °C.
quiz.explanation: Impurities lower the onset of melting and widen the melting range; a broad range (6 °C) starting 14 °C below the literature value is strong evidence of impurity, not a different compound identity or instrument error alone.

quiz.question: When drying a gravimetric precipitate to constant mass, which criterion correctly defines 'constant mass'?
options: The precipitate is heated at 105 °C for exactly 1 hour.
Two consecutive weighings after separate drying periods agree to within ±0.0002 g.
The mass does not change over 10 minutes at room temperature.
The precipitate turns white and stops steaming.
quiz.explanation: Constant mass is defined operationally as two successive drying-and-weighing cycles giving masses that agree to within ±0.0002 g (the precision limit of an analytical balance), confirming all volatile material has been removed.

quiz.question: In a formal practical report, which section should contain a statement such as 'Parallax error was minimised by reading the burette at eye level'?
options: Aim
Results table
Precautions / Sources of error
Conclusion
quiz.explanation: Statements about how errors were controlled or minimised belong in the Precautions or Sources of Error section, where the student demonstrates awareness of experimental limitations and the steps taken to reduce them.
